ECE 6390

GPS legacy signals and the navigation message

From the figure to the concept

Fig. 1 shows the legacy L1 carrier holding the narrow C/A code and the wide P(Y) code, and the nested time scales from one code chip to a 30-second message frame.

A GPS signal has three layers. The carrier places it in the RF spectrum: legacy L1 at 1575.42 MHz and L2 at 1227.60 MHz. A spreading code modulates the carrier with rapid chips; the coarse/acquisition (C/A) code runs at 1.023 Mchip/s and the precision code, encrypted as P(Y), at 10.23 Mchip/s. A slow navigation message rides on the code at 50 bit/s. Legacy L1 carries both codes; legacy L2 carries P(Y).

With rectangular chips, a code at rate R_c has a sinc² spectrum whose first nulls sit ±R_c from the carrier, a first-null width of 2R_c: 2.046 MHz for C/A and 20.46 MHz for P(Y). A chip also sets a distance scale, c/R_c: 293 m for C/A and 29.3 m for P(Y). The faster code gives finer timing and a wider spectrum without raising the message rate.

The C/A code repeats every 1023 chips, exactly 1 ms, so 20 code periods fit in each 20 ms data bit. Coherent integration longer than 20 ms may straddle a bit-sign change, so the receiver must know or remove the message bits first.

The message is organized into 300-bit subframes of 6 s and 1500-bit frames of 30 s. It carries satellite-clock corrections, the ephemeris that gives the broadcasting satellite’s precise orbit, and the almanac that gives coarser orbits for the whole constellation to guide the search for other satellites.

Example

One C/A chip lasts 1/(1.023 × 10⁶) ≈ 977.5 ns, which light crosses in 293.05 m. The code period is 1023 × 977.5 ns = 1 ms, a data bit is 20 ms, a subframe is 300 × 20 ms = 6 s, and a frame is 1500 × 20 ms = 30 s.

Practice

1. Why can a receiver that tracks only C/A on L1 not apply the two-frequency ionosphere correction by itself?

List which legacy codes appear on L2.

Legacy L2 carries only P(Y), whose encrypted code is not available to an ordinary civil receiver, so a legacy C/A receiver measures on L1 alone.

2. A receiver integrates the C/A correlation coherently for 40 ms. What must it handle that a 10 ms integration aligned within one bit can ignore?

Compare the integration time with the 20 ms data-bit duration.

A 40 ms window spans at least one data-bit boundary, where the navigation message can flip the sign of the code. The receiver must know or estimate those bit signs, or the contributions partly cancel.
